prompt_free_text:
This paper tackles an important and practically motivated problem: extracting product attributes in an open-world setting with only light supervision. The proposed setting goes beyond standard closed-world extraction and also beyond zero-shot extraction with predefined target attributes, by asking the system to both expand known seed attributes and discover previously unspecified new attribute types. This is a meaningful direction for e-commerce NLP, where attribute inventories are fluid and exhaustive annotation is expensive. The paper also contributes a new dataset, WoaM, and proposes Amacer, a pipeline combining syntax-based candidate generation, supervised contrastive learning from seed attributes, adaptive expansion for known attributes, and two forms of weak regularization for discovering new attributes. Overall, I found the paper interesting, timely, and practically relevant, with several strong ideas and a reasonably convincing empirical story. At the same time, there are some methodological and evaluation issues that limit how strongly I can endorse the claims.

The main strengths are clear. First, the task formulation is valuable. The distinction between expanding existing attribute vocabularies and discovering entirely new attribute types is well articulated, and the paper makes a good case that this is closer to real deployment needs than either closed-world tagging or zero-shot extraction with manually specified target types. Second, the dataset effort appears substantial and useful. The combination of corpus, curated seed set, and human-annotated test set is thoughtfully designed, and the inclusion of bullet points in addition to titles is especially important because richer product descriptions are indeed where many long-tail attributes live. Third, the proposed method is sensible and modular. The syntax-oriented candidate generation is simple but pragmatic; the supervised contrastive objective is cleaner than some prior metric-learning formulations; and the adaptive expansion stage is a nice way to explicitly separate seed-type expansion from residual clustering for new types. Fourth, the empirical gains over OA-Mine and other baselines are nontrivial, and the ablations suggest that both the candidate generation and the implicit regularization contribute.

I also appreciate that the paper does not oversell the current state of the problem. The qualitative examples and the span-level precision/recall analysis make it clear that open-world attribute mining remains difficult, especially for new types and for bullet-point text. The discussion of topic collapse in the latent attribute module is also refreshingly honest.

That said, I have several concerns.

The first major issue is evaluation design. The paper’s main scalar metric is a “pseudo-F1” constructed by averaging Jaccard, ARI, and NMI as a proxy for precision and combining that with recall. This is unconventional and somewhat hard to interpret. Jaccard, ARI, and NMI are clustering agreement metrics with different scales and behaviors; averaging them and calling the result “precision” is not theoretically justified. Because the paper’s headline improvements are reported in this pseudo-F1, the conclusions depend heavily on a metric whose semantics are unclear. The paper does provide the underlying clustering metrics and recall separately, which helps, but I think the central claim would be much stronger if it relied on more standard evaluation protocols for open extraction/clustering. At minimum, the paper should justify this aggregation more carefully, discuss its limitations, and show that conclusions are robust under alternative summaries. For example, reporting pairwise precision/recall/F1 over span pairs assigned to the same attribute cluster, B-cubed metrics, or V-measure alongside coverage would make the evaluation easier to trust.

Relatedly, the evaluation mixes two difficult subproblems: span detection and attribute clustering. The paper does attempt to disentangle them by evaluating with gold spans as candidates in one analysis table, which is good, but this is not emphasized enough in the main results. Since candidate generation quality has a large effect on downstream performance, it would be helpful to present a clearer decomposition in the main experimental section: candidate recall, candidate precision, clustering quality given gold spans, and end-to-end quality. As it stands, some of the gains attributed to representation learning may partly come from better candidate generation, and vice versa.

A second concern is fairness and comparability of baselines. The paper compares segmentation-based open-world methods against syntax-based methods, and also includes variants where OA-Mine is adapted to use the new candidate spans. This is useful, but the comparison still feels somewhat asymmetric. Since candidate generation is a major contribution, it is fair to compare end-to-end systems; however, when claiming superiority of the representation learning approach, the strongest comparison should hold candidate generation fixed. The OA-Mine* variant helps, but more detail is needed on whether all hyperparameters and implementation choices were carefully retuned for the new dataset and candidate regime. Similarly, the closed-world tagging baselines are expected to underperform on new-type discovery by construction, so their inclusion is mainly contextual rather than competitive. I would have liked stronger open clustering baselines on top of the same candidate spans and encoder, such as HAC, spectral clustering, constrained clustering using seeds, or nearest-prototype assignment with rejection. The current DBSCAN and DBSCAN+AE baselines are somewhat weak.

A third issue is the novelty and necessity of some components. The syntax-based candidate generation is practical, but conceptually modest. The supervised contrastive learning component is standard. The adaptive expansion thresholding is intuitive but also fairly heuristic. The most novel part is the implicit-signal regularization, especially the latent attribute module, but this component is also the least clearly validated. The paper states that the latent attribute formulation contributes around 70% of the regularization improvement, but the exact ablation evidence is not shown in the provided main tables. I would want to see a clean breakdown: supervised only, +self-supervised bullet heuristic, +latent attributes, +both, with variance across runs. I would also like more evidence that the latent attributes improve genuinely new-type discovery rather than simply smoothing embeddings. For example, does the gain concentrate on unseen types, rare values, or bullet-point spans? Some of this is hinted at in Table 4, but a more direct analysis would strengthen the claim.

The latent attribute model itself raises some questions. It is described as a neural topic-model-style regularizer over candidate spans, but the formulation seems to operate over unique candidate spans in a batch, with product-level distributions over latent attributes and attribute-level distributions over spans. This is reasonable, but several practical details are missing or underexplained. How sensitive is performance to the number of latent attributes K? How are duplicate spans across products handled? Does the model overfit frequent lexicalized spans? How stable are the learned latent attributes across runs? Since topic collapse is acknowledged, it would be useful to quantify how severe it is and whether it affects downstream performance. Without such analysis, the latent attribute module feels promising but somewhat underdeveloped.

A fourth concern is dataset scope and generalization. WoaM covers only four product categories, all from Amazon, all in English. For a first dataset this is acceptable, but the paper occasionally makes broader claims about practicality and scalability that are not fully supported by the evidence. The syntax-based candidate generation depends on POS tagging quality and on POS patterns harvested from product profiles; both may transfer imperfectly to other domains, languages, or noisier text. Likewise, the seed construction process uses retailer-provided profiles plus human curation, which is practical in some settings but may not be universally available. I do not think these are fatal limitations, but the claims should be calibrated more carefully. A cross-category transfer experiment or leave-one-category-out evaluation would have been especially informative for assessing robustness.

The annotation protocol also deserves more scrutiny. The paper says annotators label all spans that appear as reasonable attribute values of either existing or brand-new types, with no overlapping spans and one type per span. This is understandable, but “reasonable attribute values” is subjective, especially in open-world settings. The paper does not report inter-annotator agreement, adjudication details, or examples of ambiguous cases. Since the evaluation depends on clustering spans into latent attribute types, annotation consistency on type granularity is crucial. For example, distinctions like “region of origin” versus “ingredient source” or “compatibility model” versus “device family” can be subtle. More annotation details are needed to assess dataset reliability.

I also have some technical questions about the method. The supervised contrastive loss notation appears slightly unusual: the denominator seems to sum over negatives only, whereas standard supervised contrastive formulations often include all non-anchor examples. Perhaps this is intentional, but it should be clarified. The adaptive expansion threshold is based on average intra-support cosine distance scaled by delta. This assumes seed sets are internally coherent and roughly spherical; if a seed attribute is semantically broad, the threshold may become too loose, while for narrow attributes it may be too strict. Some analysis of threshold behavior across attributes would be useful. In addition, assigning candidates to existing attributes before clustering the remainder may bias the system toward over-absorbing unseen attributes into known ones, which the qualitative error analysis indeed suggests. It would be interesting to compare against a joint clustering approach with seed-informed constraints rather than a sequential pipeline.

Despite these concerns, I think the empirical section is generally solid. The gains over OA-Mine are meaningful, especially when using the same syntax-based candidates. The decomposition by seed versus new types and title versus bullet points is informative. The span-level extraction scores are also useful because they reveal that candidate generation remains a bottleneck. The qualitative examples are well chosen and support the narrative that the system can substantially expand seed vocabularies while still struggling with truly novel attribute typing.

In terms of writing, the paper is mostly clear and easy to follow, and the motivation is strong. However, there are many grammatical issues and awkward phrasings throughout the manuscript. These do not prevent understanding, but they do detract from polish. There are also a few notation inconsistencies and formatting artifacts in the equations. A careful proofreading pass would help significantly.

My overall assessment is positive but not unreserved. I believe the paper makes a worthwhile contribution through its task formulation, dataset, and practical pipeline, and I expect it would be of interest to the community working on information extraction, e-commerce NLP, and weak supervision. However, the evaluation methodology, baseline strength, and validation of the most novel regularization component need to be strengthened for the claims to be fully convincing.

If accepted, I would strongly encourage the authors to revise the paper along the following lines. First, improve the evaluation section by reducing reliance on the pseudo-F1 metric and adding more standard clustering/extraction metrics. Second, provide clearer decomposition of end-to-end performance into candidate generation and clustering quality, ideally in the main paper. Third, expand ablations for the self-supervised and latent-attribute regularizers, including sensitivity to K and run variance. Fourth, add annotation details and inter-annotator agreement for the test set. Fifth, discuss more explicitly the limitations of transfer beyond the four English Amazon categories. Finally, polish the writing and notation.

In summary, this is an interesting and practically motivated paper with promising results and a useful dataset, but with some methodological weaknesses that prevent it from being a fully definitive treatment of the problem. I lean positive overall, especially if the venue values new task settings and realistic weak-supervision formulations, but I would want the authors to address the evaluation and validation concerns in a revision.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper introduces a new lightly supervised open-world product attribute mining setting, where a model must both expand values for known seed attribute types and discover values for previously unseen attribute types without explicit type descriptions. To support this setting, the authors construct the WoaM dataset over four Amazon product categories with curated seed attributes and human-annotated test data. They propose Amacer, a pipeline consisting of syntax-based candidate span generation using POS patterns, supervised contrastive representation learning from seed attributes, adaptive expansion of seed clusters plus DBSCAN for grouping, and two additional regularizers for unseen attribute discovery: a self-supervised bullet-point co-occurrence contrastive loss and an unsupervised latent-attribute topic-model-like objective. Experiments show improvements over OA-Mine and tagging baselines on their proposed clustering-style evaluation, with especially stronger performance on new attribute types.
strengths: Addresses a practically relevant and underexplored setting between closed-world extraction and zero-shot extraction, namely open-world discovery under limited supervision.
Introduces a new dataset with curated seed supervision and explicit evaluation of unseen attribute types, including richer product text beyond titles.
The overall pipeline is intuitive and modular: candidate generation, representation learning, and clustering/grouping are clearly separated.
The use of additional implicit signals for unseen attributes is a meaningful idea; the latent-attribute regularization is a reasonable attempt to inject corpus-level semantics beyond seed labels.

Empirical gains over OA-Mine-style baselines are substantial on the authors' benchmark, and the paper includes useful ablations comparing segmentation vs syntax-based candidates and regularization vs no regularization.
The paper is generally transparent about limitations, including noisy candidate spans and topic collapse in latent attributes.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol is nonstandard and somewhat ad hoc: the main metric is a pseudo-F1 built from averaging clustering metrics and combining them with recall, which is hard to interpret and may not faithfully reflect extraction quality.

The proposed method is a pipeline with several heuristic components (POS-pattern candidate generation, adaptive thresholds, DBSCAN, bullet-point heuristic), making it difficult to isolate which innovations are fundamentally responsible for gains.
The dataset is limited to only four product categories from Amazon, raising concerns about generalization across domains, languages, and broader ecommerce settings.
Candidate span quality remains weak, as acknowledged by the authors; exact span F1 is below 37, suggesting that downstream clustering improvements may be constrained by noisy extraction.

Comparison to prior work is not entirely clean because some baselines are adapted to a different candidate generation regime, and the proposed syntax-based candidate generator itself appears to contribute a large fraction of the gains.
The paper does not provide enough analysis of sensitivity to key hyperparameters such as the number of latent attributes K, DBSCAN parameters, threshold relaxation delta, or regularization weights.
methodological_flaws: The supervised contrastive loss appears mathematically mis-specified. In the denominator of Eq. for L^su, the sum is over N^s(i)=I^s\P^s(i), which seems to include the anchor i itself unless explicitly excluded; standard supervised contrastive formulations also include positives in the denominator. As written, the objective deviates from the cited formulation and may be incorrect or at least ambiguously defined.

The self-supervised contrastive loss has the same issue: the denominator over N^b(i) excludes positives but the formulation is not the standard InfoNCE/supervised contrastive form, and it is unclear whether the anchor itself is excluded. This weakens confidence in the mathematical correctness of the training objective.

The latent-attribute variational formulation is under-specified and partly inconsistent. Eq. (3) predicts mean/variance via a linear map, but variance must be constrained positive; the paper does not state whether log-variance, softplus, or another parameterization is used. The KL term in Eq. (8) is written as KL(\tilde{\alpha}^p || \hat{\alpha}), but \tilde{\alpha}^p is sampled Gaussian logits while \hat{\alpha} is described as a standard Gaussian prior over product-to-attribute distribution; the notation conflates Gaussian latent variables with softmax-normalized attribute probabilities, making the probabilistic model unclear.

The reconstruction objective in the latent-attribute model uses only observed candidate spans in V(p) without discussing normalization for repeated spans, negative sampling, or bag-of-spans counts. This makes empirical validity of the topic-model analogy uncertain and may bias toward frequent spans.

The main empirical claim of open-world discovery is weakened by the evaluation design. Because clustering metrics are computed only on matched gold spans and then combined with recall into a pseudo-F1, the metric may obscure failure modes such as over-fragmentation, over-merging, or extraction of many noisy spans. The paper itself reports low span precision/recall, indicating that the main metric may overstate practical extraction quality.

Statistical significance claims are insufficiently supported. The paper mentions a t-test with >95% confidence, but it is unclear what the sample units are (categories, runs, or examples). With only four product categories, a t-test is not very convincing unless multiple independent runs are reported.

The adaptive expansion threshold uses average intra-support cosine distance as a threshold. Since cosine is referred to as a distance in Eq. (1)-(2) but elsewhere dot product/cosine similarity is used as similarity, the sign convention is ambiguous. If cosine distance means 1-cosine similarity, then lower is better; if cosine means similarity, the inequality direction would be reversed. This ambiguity affects reproducibility and scientific clarity.
